title: I’m paying him to suck (for now)

conversation.headline: I’m paying him to suck (for now)
paragraphs: A few months ago, I told Eli Treff that you’re going to face judgment when you start something new. Nobody steps onto the court as Michael Jordan. It takes years of practice to get there.
I didn’t think much about that line again until now, because now I’m on the other side of it.

I’m training a new salesperson, and I keep catching myself rushing him. Jumping into a call to give advice. Getting antsy while he’s talking, for no real reason. Wanting to move to the next step before he’s had a chance to be bad at this one.

I’ve asked myself why. Part of it is that I don’t want him to look bad. Part of it is money: I’m paying him a salary, and I want it to pay off. But mostly it’s my own discomfort watching someone struggle.

Here’s what that costs. When I rush him, I’m trying to move the needle somewhere it can’t move yet. He doesn’t have the skills or the knowledge. And I never find out where he needs work, because I covered the gap before it showed.

I know how this works because of how I started. I was terrible at sales. I was afraid to reach out to anyone. When I decided to take on my social anxiety, I gave myself one small goal for my first event: talk to three people. I didn’t even have to say what I do. Just “My name is Ami Morgenstern.”
That’s how I got moving: one small step at a time.
conversation.takeaway: Letting him be less profitable right now is the more profitable move long term. The struggle isn’t a cost. It’s the diagnosis.
conversation.clipLabel: Short clip: Embrace judgment for growth

build.headline: Record the call. Then make him listen.
paragraphs: Moishe, our new salesman, made a cold call this week and someone actually picked up. That almost never happens. I wasn’t in the room.
So I asked him to play the call back. He said no. He couldn’t stand hearing himself.
I get it. Nobody likes hearing themselves. I made him listen anyway.
Then I asked one question: what would you do differently? He had answers. I didn’t have to tell him what went wrong, because he heard it himself. On the next call, we had a game plan.

That’s the loop I’m building into training: make the call, listen back, let him name what he’d change, and walk into the next call with one specific thing to try. It’s not about the sucking. It’s about not wasting the rep.
build.takeaway: Pick one thing you do repeatedly, such as a call, a pitch, or a client meeting, and record it this week. Listen back and ask yourself the same question: what would I do differently?

thinking.headline: Caring about a number doesn’t earn it a line
paragraphs: This week I helped a friend who was asking whether he should hire a fractional CFO. I asked him what for. He told me, “Because I don’t know how to read my reports.”
So I looked at his reports. His P&L wasn’t bloated. But when I asked how he decided what goes on it, he had nothing. No rule, no framework. The lines were just there.

At first, I thought the test was simple: do you care about that number? That’s not good enough. You can care about a lot of numbers. Caring, by itself, is not a good enough reason for something to make it onto the P&L.

If splitting out a service would change what you do (how you price it, whether you push it, whether you keep offering it at all), track it separately. If you’d do the exact same thing either way, it’s just extra detail cluttering up the report.
thinking.takeaway: The only good enough reason is this: are decisions being made off that number?
